headlines.article_text: BP’s third-quarter profit nearly quadruples as refining margins surge Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points BP’s underlying profit nearly quadrupled year on year to $8.5 billion in the third quarter, beating analyst expectations of $6.19 billion. The company cited stronger gas and marketing trading and significantly higher refining margins. Refining margins surged as supply disruptions tightened fuel markets, but CEO Meg O’Neill said BP expects some easing in the fourth quarter. BP is strengthening its balance sheet to support shareholder returns through the cycle. Operating cash flow rose to $28.55 billion in the first nine months, from $16.89 billion a year earlier, while net debt fell to $13.87 billion. O’Neill said the company is also setting aside extra cash for its remaining obligations over the Deepwater Horizon disaster. In this article BP Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 7:56 07:56 BP CEO: The macro environment is a tailwind Squawk Box Europe Oil major BP smashed third-quarter expectations on Friday, as volatile energy markets and high refining margins saw profits nearly quadruple year-on-year. The company reported $8.5 billion in underlying replacement cost profit, used as a proxy for net profit. That was above the $6.191 billion forecast by analysts in an LSEG-compiled consensus and up from $2.2 billion a year ago . Operating cash flow hit $28.55 billion across the first nine months of the year, up from $16.89 billion in 2025, while net debt fell to $13.87 billion from $26.05 billion across the same period. The result primarily reflects better performance in gas and marketing trading, and "significantly higher" realized refining margins, BP said. "These are dynamic times with volatility and disruption to trade flows continuing to define energy markets," BP CEO Meg O'Neill said in a statement. "The industry as a whole has been showing remarkable adaptability. Refineries have been running close to capacity to make up for shortfalls, shipping has been taking different and longer routes, and releases from strategic and commercial reserves are helping to bridge supply gap." Demand outlook Rivals Shell and TotalEnergies on Thursday said their refining margins — the amount earned from processing crude oil into products like diesel, jet fuel and gasoline — hit historically high levels . Outages and damage to refineries from global conflicts, from the Russia-Ukraine war to the Middle East, have created tightness in global fuel markets this year, pushing product prices sharply higher relative to crude . Benchmark crude prices have also been hugely volatile this year as traders reacted swiftly to unpredictable newsflow coming from the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran, and remain nearly double their level a year ago. ICE Brent crude price. Analysts have been questioning when and if high energy prices will ultimately drive demand destruction, easing pressures on constrained refineries, as the premium for refined products over crude remains at decade-highs. BP CEO O'Neill told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday that BP's refining indicator margin for the quarter of $46.7 a barrel was "incredibly strong" and "indicative of demand for the products we produce," boosted by refining reliability of over 96%. "We've been able to adapt and try to adjust our refining runs to meet... the needs for the product that is most in demand," she said. "Now, if we roll forward, we are seeing refining margins start to soften a bit ... third quarter is always a big driving period and a big holiday period. So, fourth quarter demand typically drops off. That is bringing the refining margins down a bit." "But again, what we control is our ability to run our facilities safely and reliably to try to capture the opportunity that presents itself." BP announced a new strategy last year that sees the energy giant pivot back towards its traditional oil and gas operations and away from renewables. It also announced a consolidation of its leadership structure and debt reduction. O'Neill told CNBC on Friday that BP was focused on strengthening its balance sheet to give shareholders "confidence that they can be rewarded through the cycle." "So, oil prices today are strong. They will not always be strong. I've got 30 years in the industry, and the prices go up and down. And at some point, they will fall again. So we need to design a company and a financial frame and a balance sheet that allows us to reward shareholders through the cycle." That includes addressing its financial obligations, including the $5.9 billion it still owes the U.S. government and states for settlements over the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010 , which it intends to ringfence extra cash for, she said. "Deepwater Horizon was an incredible tragedy, and it has shaped BP. We will not forget the 11 men who lost their lives, or the impact that we had on the Gulf Coast and the environment there," she said. "So we have deeply embedded those lessons, but we're in a position now where we want to take care of those financial obligations going forward to ensure we're a more resilient company in future years." headlines.article_text: Novartis remibrutinib MS drug faces efficacy questions Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan told CNBC on Tuesday that its drug remibrutinib could become "one of our largest medicines in history." But analysts slashed the peak sales forecast for the drug after a late-stage clinical trial for patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while reaching its primary endpoint, appeared worse than expected. It comes as Novartis reported improved profitability in the third quarter, as it emerges from the steepest patent cliff in its history. In this article NVS XPH Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT "This medicine could be one of our largest medicines in history," Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan told CNBC on Tuesday, as the Swiss drugmaker backed remibrutinib, its experimental MS medicine, to generate more than $4 billion in peak annual sales. Days before, Barclays cut its forecast for the drug's peak sales after detailed results from two late-stage trials showed the drug had reduced relapses in MS patients by less than analysts expected. It highlights a challenge for Novartis as it prepares to outline its long-term growth strategy in mid-November. The drugmaker reported sales growth this week despite losing key patent protection for blockbuster heart drug Entresto. But Barclays analysts said that the market is already looking to the next patent cliff, with bestsellers Kisqali and Kesimpta facing patent expirations around 2032. watch now VIDEO 3:14 03:14 Novartis CEO: We have the “replacement power” ahead of patent cliff Squawk Box Europe That's "the market's bigger question," Barclays analysts said on Wednesday, noting Kisqali and Kesimpta expiries alone represent $18 billion in peak sales. Against that backdrop, Novartis has guided for $8 billion-plus in total sales of remibrutinib, including indications other than relapsing MS. Amit Bar-Or, a multiple sclerosis specialist at the University of Pennsylvania, told CNBC that remibrutinib appeared to offer a promising safety profile but was unlikely to control relapsing MS as effectively as high-efficacy antibodies like Novartis' own Kesimpta. He added that the drug's biggest opportunity to expand the market could emerge if ongoing trials demonstrate a benefit in progressive multiple sclerosis, where treatment options remain limited. How remibrutinib works Remibrutinib belongs to a class of medicines known as BTK inhibitors, which aim to reduce the immune system activity that damages nerves in MS patients. Kesimpta works differently. It is a monoclonal antibody that binds to the CD20 protein, depleting B cells involved in the autoimmune response in MS. Unlike Kesimpta, remibrutinib aims to regulate the cells' activity without eliminating them. Bar-Or distinguished the biology of relapsing MS — in which patients experience flare-ups — from progressive MS, which worsens gradually over time. Clinical results for remibrutinib in relapsing MS appear to be similar to Roche's rival BTK inhibitor fenebrutinib, but less effective at preventing relapses than anti-CD20 treatments such as Kesimpta, according to Bar-Or. No head-to-head trials have yet compared remibrutinib with fenebrutinib or anti-CD20 treatments, making direct comparisons difficult. It could still be an attractive switch for patients who are experiencing progressive MS while on an anti-CD20, he added. An ongoing clinical trial testing whether remibrutinib can effectively treat progressive MS is expected to read out in 2031. One potential advantage of BTK inhibitors is that they regulate immune cells rather than eliminate them, which could make them safer over the long term than some existing MS treatments, Bar-Or said. However, there is not yet enough long-term safety data to confirm this, he added. Cholesterol drug setback casts doubt over multibillion-dollar race A Novartis spokesperson told CNBC that it views remibrutinib primarily as an opportunity to expand its MS portfolio, rather than replace sales of Kesimpta. The company is targeting newly diagnosed patients, those currently taking oral treatments, and patients receiving anti-CD20 therapies who may be eligible to switch. Novartis sees a $6 billion-plus peak annual sales opportunity for Kesimpta alongside $4 billion-plus for remibrutinib in relapsing MS. Remibrutinib sales outlook Morningstar analyst Jay Lee told CNBC that Novartis' $4 billion-plus peak sales forecast for remibrutinib in MS was "within the realm of possibility" but wasn't "de-risked." Lee added that this would depend on how remibrutinib compares with Roche's rival fenebrutinib, drug pricing negotiations, whether its potential tolerability advantages translate into patients staying on treatment longer, and whether clinical trials support switching patients from existing MS treatments. "In the near term, I expect the largest market for remibrutinib will be the oral switch market, i.e. patients taking a generic oral treatment who need to switch, particularly due to tolerability reasons." While that could allow remibrutinib to take some market share from CD20 drugs like Ocrevus and Kesimpta, it "may still work in Novartis' favor if it means they gain overall RMS patient share from Roche, which currently leads the market," Lee said, adding that Novartis estimates about 75% of switch-eligible patients on CD20 drugs are not on Kesimpta. Additionally, remibrutinib is already approved to treat certain forms of chronic hives, and a late-stage clinical trial testing it for the chronic inflammatory skin disease hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is expected to read out before Nov. 19. Barclays estimates a $2 billion peak annual sales opportunity in HS but assigns the drug only a 50% probability of success, citing an unusual dose-response pattern in mid-stage trials and a history of late-stage trial failures in HS.
